title: Mr. 3000
full_review:
In "Mr. 3000" (Touchstone), a baseball comedy about an aging ballplayer who comes out of retirement to guarantee his place in the record books, director Charles Stone III swings for the feel-good fences but comes up short of a home run.
Bernie Mac stars as Stan Ross, an arrogant all-star with a sweet swing and a sour attitude, playing for the hapless Milwaukee Brewers.

On the night he joins the exclusive 3,000-hit club -- one of the rarest milestones in all professional sports -- Ross hangs up his cleats, leaving his teammates in the lurch.

Confident that his ticket to the Hall of Fame has been punched, Ross capitalizes on his self-aggrandizing moniker, turning it into a "Mr. 3000" retail empire, as he waits for Cooperstown to call.

But nine years later, an error in recordkeeping is discovered, revealing that he had only accrued 2,997 base hits -- three shy of the landmark number he has built his entire identity around -- putting his hopes of a bronze plaque on hold.

Out of shape and over the hill, Ross decides to pull the baseball equivalent of a George Foreman and re-signs with his former team -- still mired in its losing ways -- in order to scrape together the three hits. Struggling to regain his old form, he quickly becomes a joke to the press, a curiosity to the fans and a ticket draw to the team's ownership (headed by Chris Noth).

What starts out as a pursuit of personal accolades becomes a humbling quest for personal redemption, as he begins to reassess his priorities. Along the way, Ross' old-school passion rubs off on his young teammates, predictably transforming them from a locker room of underachievers into believers. Only this time around the bases, Ross won't make the same mistakes. Or will he?
While not in the same league as films like "Field of Dreams," "Bull Durham" and "The Natural," "Mr. 3000" has a certain crowd-pleasing charm.

Mac steps up to the plate for the first time in a leading role. And while it is hardly a grand-slam performance, he takes his swings with authority and doesn't strike out. Angela Bassett is wasted as a sassy ESPN reporter who once had a fling with Ross and is now covering his comeback. The same goes for Paul Sorvino as the near-mute Milwaukee manager.

The implausibility of the premise aside, the baseball sequences -- shot on location in Milwaukee's Miller Park -- are convincing, their believability enhanced by the casting of actors with real sports experience in supporting roles, including ex-pro football player Brian White as the Brew crew's hot-dogging superstar-on-the-rise, T-Rex.

Though all-star names like Denzel Washington and John Travolta had been tossed around during the script's 10-year development, relative rookie Mac's comedic charisma softens the character's more abrasive edges and succeeds in making even a self-absorbed braggart likable. Mac also provides many of the film's genuine laughs.

Unfortunately much of the picture's humor is of the vulgar and sexually suggestive variety, which is unwelcome in a PG-13 movie. Still, the ultimate message imparted is one of self-sacrifice over selfishness and everyone deserving a second chance.
If one can look past its cliches and unnecessary crudeness, "Mr. 3000" offers viewers diverting entertainment.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, fleeting partial rear nudity and recurring coarse language and humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
